newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen opening slightly off in quiet day.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen opening slightly off in quiet day.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are seen opening mixed to slightly lower Monday, with markets hesitant to do much of anything until the Federal Reserve gives guidance on interest rates at its meeting tomorrow.
Stocks ended sharply lower Friday on renewed fears that the Fed would raise short-term rates.
The Standard & Poors Futures index was trading down 0.50 point at 831.55 and the long bond was unchanged at a yield of 6.91 percent. U.S. stocks were quiet in London due to holidays in Europe.

"Given the fact that everything is on hold until tomorrow, I don't see much of anything happening, though stocks could open with a slight tilt to the downside," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities.

The Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's policy-making arm, meets tomorrow. Analysts are divided over whether the FOMC will boost rates and whether the stock market has already adjusted share valuations to account for a rate rise.
No economic data were due out Monday that might give the stock market a clear direction.
"I think today will be an assessment day," Peter Cardillo, an analyst at Westfalia Investments, said. "The markets will do little of anything either way with everyone on Fed watch."
Cardillo believes the Fed will raise interest rates but that this will not hurt share prices because the market has already factored in a 25 basis point rate rise.
Other analysts expect a volatile week, saying the stock market is vulnerable and not prepared for a hike.
At its last meeting on March 25 the FOMC raised short-term rates for the first time in more than two years, bumping them up by a quarter percentage point.
Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average gained 165.02 points, or 0.81 percent, at 20,489.75.
In London the FTSE 100 was off 37 points at 4657. U.S. stocks were quiet in London, with trading restricted by public holidays in many European centers.
The dollar recovered against the yen in Tokyo, trading at 116.08/13 after falling as low as 114.85, and was at 1.7023/33 marks in Europe.
The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column said some News Corp investors wish Rupert Murdoch would stop buying firms and try to run what he already owns.
The New York Times's market place column said the stock of Informix Corp has been hurt because takeover candidates have not appeared and the company's financial situation has deteriorated.
